payload.named_tools_expected: Yes. Roughly half the AU page-one results are AI vow generators or 'best AI writers' lists that name tools (ChatGPT, Jasper, Claude, Easy-Peasy, Verble). Per run-log decision we do not rank third-party tools. Recommendation: name ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini once as examples of general assistants (as our live /expert-advice/chatgpt-vs-ai-wedding-planner already does), with no ranking, pricing or feature claims.
cross_market_insights: All four markets show an AI Overview at position 1; snippet-led answers win.

Sydney and London lead with backlash stories (Reddit, YouTube, Facebook): the dominant emotional intent is 'will my partner or guests think less of me?'. Nobody answers it with practical rules (tell your partner, write the raw material yourself).
Melbourne and Brisbane are dominated by tools and tool lists, mostly dated or self-promotional.
No top-3 result in any market covers the legal words (Marriage Act s45(2) in Australia, registrar rules in England) or that AI cannot know your celebrant's ceremony.
No top-3 result covers privacy (what you paste into a chatbot about your partner).
No top-3 result shows a worked before and after edit; the one sample visible (relationshipfire) is itself generic.
Only AU competitor with a method is The Celebrant Directory (rank 4 Sydney); it offers one prompt and tips, no legal or abroad notes.
PAA 'What to avoid when writing vows?' and 'Should I say I vow or I promise?' appear in Melbourne, Brisbane and London: answer both inside the editing section.
payload.recommended_angle: AI as a drafting partner, not a ghostwriter: you supply the stories, AI supplies structure, then you edit out what sounds like AI, check length aloud, keep the legal words intact and keep private details out of the chat.
